articleBlocks: World and Davis look like event names more than objects, which is why the board can feel sporty but still vague at first. The opening clues stay ambiguous until Stanley gives the board a cleaner test, so this guide starts with the misleading first read, then uses the later clues to show why the final connection is narrower than the early guesses and how each clue checks that same pattern without relying on the answer reveal too early.
Solheim and Webb Ellis keep the sports angle alive, yet the exact connector can stay hidden if you focus on the tournaments instead of the hardware.

fullAnalysis: World, Davis, and Solheim all feel like competition names first, which can make the board read like a list of events rather than a category of objects.
Webb Ellis continues that sports framing while adding a slightly less universal clue, which keeps the connector just out of reach.
Stanley is the turning clue because Stanley Cup is such a famous trophy name that it brings the shared word Cup into focus immediately.
After that, World Cup, Solheim Cup, Webb Ellis Cup, and Davis Cup all resolve as trophies rather than just tournaments.
The board is strong because it hides the award category behind sports labels that many people know primarily as events.
solutionNarrative: The early clues felt like competitions, not objects. World and Davis especially can make you think of tournament calendars rather than the awards themselves.
Stanley changed the perspective. Once Stanley Cup surfaced, the rest of the board stopped being about sports events and turned into a list of named trophies.
